lineages.title: The Trombone
lineages.intro:
In the New Orleans band the trombone played underneath: Kid Ory filled the gaps below the cornet with slides and smears, a style called tailgate. The swing era made it a soloist, smooth and singing in Jack Teagarden's hands, talkative and full of tricks in Dicky Wells's. Bebop was harder, because a slide is slow for fast lines; J.J. Johnson's answer, clean tonguing that made the trombone sound almost like a valve instrument, became the model most modern players followed, and the rest defined themselves against it.

Listen for the slide: how much each player smears between notes, and how much they hide it.

players.idea: Tailgate trombone: rhythmic slides and smears under the cornet, the New Orleans band's bass line in brass.
The trombone as a blues singer: long, smooth lines with the slide almost hidden.
A talking trombone: rips, slurs and growls placed with a comedian's timing in Count Basie's band.
Bebop on the trombone: clean, tongued notes at speed, so the slide sounded like valves.
Charlie Parker's lines on the slide, smooth and unpredictable, in Mingus's bands.
A warm, round hard-bop sound, with Art Blakey's Messengers and on Coltrane's Blue Train.

links.note: Teagarden never played the tailgate style Ory had made the trombone's job; he played long, smooth solos the way a trumpeter would.
Wells and Trummy Young were the first trombonists Johnson admired; he loved Wells's playing, he said, for its minimum of articulation.
As a boy in a Detroit orphanage, Fuller was taken to hear Illinois Jacquet's band with Johnson on trombone; Johnson became his main model.
Knepper said most modern trombonists imitated J.J.; his own influences weren't trombonists at all, but Charlie Parker, whose solos he transcribed.

lineages.title: The Clarinet
lineages.intro:
The clarinet was the New Orleans band's high voice, weaving around the cornet's melody. Johnny Dodds and Sidney Bechet both took lessons from the Creole Tio family of clarinetists, and the records the New Orleans players made in Chicago in the 1920s reached a teenage Benny Goodman there. In the swing era the clarinet led the most popular bands in America; after bebop it moved to the edges, where Eric Dolphy made the bass clarinet a solo voice and Anat Cohen made the clarinet sound new again.

Listen for the tone, dark and woody low down, bright and piercing at the top, and then for the vibrato: wide and fast in New Orleans, narrower or gone later.

players.idea: The New Orleans blues clarinet: a big, dark tone and crying phrases in Oliver's and Armstrong's bands.
A clarinetist before he was a saxophonist: a huge tone and a wide, fast vibrato that led any band he was in.
Swing's clarinet: a clean, centred tone and fast, even runs, in front of a big band and in small groups.
A clarinetist with a composer's ambitions: a pure, soaring top register, strings, and a concerto of his own.
Made the bass clarinet a solo instrument: honks, cries and wide leaps across its whole range.
The bass clarinet as atmosphere: dark, slow-moving lines inside the electric bands of Miles Davis and Herbie Hancock.
A warm, singing clarinet at home in New Orleans jazz, Brazilian choro and modern small groups.

links.note: Goodman grew up in Chicago listening to its New Orleans clarinetists, Dodds among them, and said no one ever surpassed Dodds's tone.
Rivals at the top of swing with different aims: Shaw recalled telling Goodman he was too hung up on the clarinet, while Shaw was trying to play music.
Cohen started on clarinet in a Dixieland band in Tel Aviv, and names Bechet, with John Coltrane, as her two great heroes growing up.
Goodman was Cohen's first introduction to jazz clarinet; for his centenary she played his repertoire in her Clarinetwork band at the Village Vanguard.
Maupin heard Dolphy and met him in Detroit, where Dolphy gave him a flute lesson; Dolphy's bass clarinet showed him what the instrument could do.

lineages.title: The Vibraphone
lineages.intro:
The vibraphone was a 1920s novelty, metal bars over tubes with a motor that makes the sound pulse. Red Norvo had already shown on xylophone and marimba how quietly a mallet instrument could swing; Lionel Hampton, a drummer, made the vibes a jazz voice in Benny Goodman's quartet. Milt Jackson slowed the pulse down and played bebop and the blues on it, and nearly every vibraphonist since comes from him or from Gary Burton, who played it like a piano with four mallets.

Listen for the shimmer, how long each player lets notes ring, and count the mallets: two for horn-like lines, four for chords.

players.idea: Chamber jazz on mallets: a light, quiet touch on xylophone and marimba, then a trio with guitar and bass instead of drums.
Made the vibraphone a jazz instrument: a drummer's drive, hard riffs and swing in the Goodman Quartet.
Bebop and the blues on vibes: a slow, warm vibrato and long, singing lines.
Brought the vibes into Latin jazz: cool, clear lines over Cuban rhythm.
Open, ringing chords and fast, modern lines: the vibes in Blue Note's 1960s avant-garde.
Four mallets and piano voicings: the vibraphone as a full harmony instrument, in duets and country-tinged jazz.
Two mallets, little pedal, and a band that talks across different pulses.

links.note: Jackson took up the vibraphone at sixteen after hearing Hampton with Benny Goodman's band.
Tjader named Hampton as his first inspiration on vibes, before Milt Jackson became his model.
Tjader said Jackson influenced him strongly; his cool, bluesy lines on the Latin dates come from Bags.
As a boy Hutcherson heard Jackson play Bemsha Swing on a Miles Davis record and decided to take up the vibraphone.
Burton called Norvo his great example; on his 2001 tribute For Hamp, Red, Bags, and Cal he re-created Norvo's 1950s trio.
Ross grew up on Jackson's records and names him as his formative influence on the instrument; like Jackson, he plays with two mallets.
At eighteen Ross visited Hutcherson at home in California; Hutcherson told him to write about his own life, advice Ross says he took literally.

lineages.title: The Organ
lineages.intro:
Fats Waller recorded jazz on the pipe organ in the 1920s, but the Hammond became a jazz instrument of its own in the 1950s. Wild Bill Davis led some of the first organ trios, with guitar and drums; Jimmy Smith played the Hammond with a bebop horn player's speed, the bass line on the lower keyboard, and the organ trio became the sound of soul jazz. Larry Young took it into Coltrane's modal world and fusion, and Joey DeFrancesco brought it back to the centre of jazz at the end of the 1980s.

Listen to the left hand and the pedals: they play the bass, so the organist is half the rhythm section too. Then listen for the drawbars and the rotating speaker, which make the sound swell and whirl.

players.idea: Jazz on the pipe organ in the 1920s and on the Hammond in 1942, with stride's bounce in both.
An early Hammond trio leader, with guitar and drums, who gave the organ the punch of a big band.
Made the Hammond B-3 a jazz instrument: bebop speed in the right hand, walking bass in the left, the blues all through.
Soul jazz with a light, crisp touch, trading choruses with tenor saxophonists.
The blues and gospel organ: a big, churchy sound and grooves built for dancing.
Took the organ into Coltrane's modal world, then fusion: open chords and long, floating lines.
Church organ and funk: slow-building grooves, swelling chords and the Hammond's wildest sounds.
Brought the organ back to jazz in the late 1980s, playing Jimmy Smith's language at a blazing pace.

links.note: Davis took Waller and Art Tatum as his early models, before he moved from piano and guitar to the organ.
Smith switched from piano to organ for good in 1954 after hearing Davis play.
Lonnie Smith remembered hearing Davis on the radio first, then Jimmy Smith; he learned from Davis's records and from the church organ.
After Davis came Jimmy Smith's records, which Lonnie Smith immersed himself in as a young player in Buffalo.
Scott said Jackie Davis and Jimmy Smith were the first two organists who inspired her to take up the instrument.
Smith was a childhood friend; McGriff took private lessons from him, and from Milt Buckner, after buying his first Hammond in 1956.
Young's first records were soul jazz in Smith's manner; at Blue Note from 1964 he turned toward Coltrane.
DeFrancesco was playing Smith's records note for note at five; Smith became his mentor and recorded with him on Incredible! and Legacy.

artists.name: Jack Teagarden
artists.blurb: A Texan who made the trombone sound like a blues singer, with long, smooth lines and a technique he largely taught himself, and who sang in the same lazy drawl. He was the trombone and second voice of Louis Armstrong's All Stars from 1947 to 1951.
signatureTracks: I Gotta Right to Sing the Blues
artists.videoQuery: Jack Teagarden trombone Basin Street Blues

artists.name: Dicky Wells
artists.blurb: Count Basie's trombonist from 1938, with a vocabulary of slurs, rips and growls that made his solos sound like speech. In Paris in 1937 he led a session with Django Reinhardt and Bill Coleman, his solos full of jokes and surprises.
signatureTracks: Between the Devil and the Deep Blue Sea

artists.name: Gary Burton
artists.blurb: Burton played the vibraphone with four mallets, voicing chords like a pianist, and his 1967 quartet record Duster mixed jazz with country and rock before fusion had a name. His duets with Chick Corea ran for forty years, and he taught at Berklee for thirty.

artists.name: Wild Bill Davis
artists.blurb: Louis Jordan's pianist turned organist, who led one of the first Hammond trios from 1950 and set the instrument's pace until Jimmy Smith arrived. His arrangement of April in Paris became Count Basie's 1955 hit.

notes: TROMBONE: six players, four links, and two of the links are weaker than the standard you asked for. (1) Kid Ory → Jack Teagarden is marked 'reaction' on historians' framing (Wikipedia's Teagarden article and Scott Yanow), not on anything Teagarden said; I found no documented Ory → Teagarden influence or bandmate relationship (they shared the stage at Newport in 1957, which isn't enough). If the reviewer drops it, Teagarden is left without a link and the tree falls to five linked players. (2) Jack Teagarden → J.J. Johnson is NOT drawn: in Johnson's own interviews (Bernotas 1999; Universalis) the trombonists he names are Dicky Wells, Trummy Young, J.C. Higginbotham and Fred Beckett, never Teagarden.

TROMBONE: Dicky Wells is a second proposed new artist (entry in `artists`), added because he is the trombonist J.J. Johnson named, which gives the bebop branch a documented root in the swing era. Wikipedia gives his birth year as '1907 or 1909'; I used 1907. On Apple Music his records are credited variously to 'Dicky Wells', 'Dickie Wells', 'Dicky Wells & Bill Coleman' and 'Dicky Wells and His Orchestra'.

TROMBONE: Trombone Shorty is left out. Asked about his trombone heroes, he points to Rebirth Brass Band and, through them, the JB Horns, and his named mentors (Cyril Neville, Wynton Marsalis, Kermit Ruffins, Allen Toussaint, Lenny Kravitz) aren't trombonists in jazz.json. No documented link reaches anyone in this tree, so the tree stops at Fuller and Knepper (1950s-60s). Adding Rebirth Brass Band, Fred Wesley or Delfeayo Marsalis would be the way to reach him.

TROMBONE: J.J. Johnson's track is 'J.J. Johnson|Blue Trombone' (1957, on Apple Music as 'Blue Trombone (Part 1 & 2)' and on The Trombone Master). It is NOT in his signatureTracks: those three (Manteca Theme, Boplicity, Moon Dreams) are ensemble pieces where he is barely featured, so it's worth adding Blue Trombone to his signatureTracks. Jimmy Knepper's 'Fables of Faubus' is from Mingus Ah Um: Wikipedia's personnel lists Knepper on tracks 1 and 7 (Better Git It in Your Soul, Fables of Faubus) and Willie Dennis on the others.

CLARINET: Jimmy Giuffre is left out. I found no documented link between him and any clarinetist in the cast (his named model is Lester Young on tenor, and even that is secondary), and Giuffre's own words weren't findable. Eric Dolphy (bass clarinet; already in the saxophone tree) and Bennie Maupin (instrument 'Clarinet' in jazz.json, bass clarinet on Bitches Brew) are in instead, as a second branch with its own documented link. That branch doesn't connect to the New Orleans/swing branch.

CLARINET: Sidney Bechet's track 'Egyptian Fantasy' (1941, Victor, on Apple Music as 'Sidney Bechet|Egyptian Fantasy') is NOT in his signatureTracks, which are all soprano saxophone features (Summertime, Petite Fleur, Wild Cat Blues). I chose it because it's a clarinet feature; please confirm by ear that it's the clarinet take before shipping. The fallback is 'Sidney Bechet|Wild Cat Blues'. Johnny Dodds's 'Weary City' is a highlight of blue-clarinet-stomp.

CLARINET (optional improvement): Jimmie Noone isn't in jazz.json, but Wikipedia documents all three of his links: Noone studied with the young Sidney Bechet (teacher), and Goodman and Artie Shaw both named him as an influence. Adding him would connect Bechet to the swing players and give Shaw a second, gentler root.

VIBRAPHONE: Gary Burton is a proposed new artist, added so that Red Norvo has a documented heir. I found no source in which Hampton or Jackson credits Norvo. Burton's artist name varies on Apple Music ('Gary Burton', 'The Gary Burton Quartet', 'Gary Burton & Chick Corea'/'Chick Corea & Gary Burton'). The Norvo → Burton note rests on Burton's tribute album and the Dutch Wikipedia/Berklee accounts. A direct Burton interview quote would strengthen it.

VIBRAPHONE: Mulatu Astatke (Vibraphone, in jazz.json) is left out: the only connection I found is that he saw Milt Jackson in New York, which isn't an influence claim. Bobby Hutcherson's track 'Out to Lunch' is the Dolphy record's title track, from his signatureTracks.

ORGAN: Wild Bill Davis is a proposed new artist and the tree's documented root for the Hammond (Jimmy Smith switched to organ after hearing him). Fats Waller is included as the pipe-organ and early-Hammond pioneer (Jitterbug Waltz, 1942, is a Hammond record and is in his signatureTracks); his link to Davis rests on one Wikipedia sentence ('took inspiration from Fats Waller and Art Tatum'), which may refer to piano. The note says 'early models', not organ specifically. Waller's instrument in jazz.json is Piano; he'd need 'Organ' in a future `instruments` list. Apple Music titles for Davis's third signature track vary ('Azure-te (Paris Blues)', 'Azure 'Te').

ORGAN: John Medeski is left out: the only artist in jazz.json is the group Medeski Martin & Wood, and Jimmy Smith's Wikipedia lists MMW (the band) among those Smith influenced, not Medeski himself. A group can't stand as an organist in the tree. Data note: jazz.json has Jimmy Smith born 1925; Wikipedia currently says 8 December 1928 (sources disagree).

All four trees use only the kinds already in use (influence, teacher, reaction). Every link either goes forward in time or is a reaction. Every player in every tree has at least one link. Notes paraphrase; the exact quotes are in `sources`.

New artist entries have `albums: []` and no `died` key for living artists. Every signatureTrack was confirmed on the US iTunes Search API (entity=song), including Teagarden: Basin Street Blues, St. James Infirmary, I Gotta Right to Sing the Blues, each with multiple Jack Teagarden-credited results. Teagarden's Wikipedia title is Jack_Teagarden.
